items.stem: Which of the following best describes "critical angle"?
options: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal
Image height divided by object height
The angle of incidence in the denser medium at which the angle of refraction is 90°
The change of direction of light when it passes from one transparent medium to another because its speed changes
items.answer: The angle of incidence in the denser medium at which the angle of refraction is 90°
items.markingKey: C. "critical angle" is the angle of incidence in the denser medium at which the angle of refraction is 90°.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "halogen displacement reaction"?
options: J. J. Thomson’s 1904 model of the atom as a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it
A reaction in which a more reactive halogen takes the place of a less reactive halogen in a compound
The percentage of atoms of an element that are a particular isotope in a natural sample
The group 17 elements (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine): reactive non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules
items.answer: A reaction in which a more reactive halogen takes the place of a less reactive halogen in a compound
items.markingKey: B. "halogen displacement reaction" is a reaction in which a more reactive halogen takes the place of a less reactive halogen in a compound.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The time at which the reaction stops because one reactant has been used up"?
items.answer: end point (of a reaction)
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of end point (of a reaction).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "variation"?
options: A characteristic controlled by a gene carried on a sex chromosome, usually the X chromosome
The combination of alleles an organism has for a gene, e.g. Bb
A genetic cross that follows the inheritance of a single gene
Differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species
items.answer: Differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species
items.markingKey: D. "variation" is differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The speed of all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s"?
items.answer: speed of light (c)
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of speed of light (c).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "chromosome"?
options: The entire genetic material of an organism
A long, coiled molecule of DNA (with proteins) found in the nucleus that carries many genes
A mass of cells formed by uncontrolled mitosis
The longest stage of the cell cycle, in which the cell grows, makes new organelles and replicates its DNA
items.answer: A long, coiled molecule of DNA (with proteins) found in the nucleus that carries many genes
items.markingKey: B. "chromosome" is a long, coiled molecule of DNA (with proteins) found in the nucleus that carries many genes.

items.stem: Lukas writes: "Exothermic reactions do not need activation energy because they give out energy." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: All reactions need activation energy to break bonds and start; exothermic reactions release more energy than they take in overall.
items.markingKey: All reactions need activation energy to break bonds and start; exothermic reactions release more energy than they take in overall. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how a catalyst increases the rate of reaction.
items.answer: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful; the catalyst is not used up. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful; the catalyst is not used up. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between mitosis and meiosis.
items.answer: Mitosis: one division, two diploid daughter cells, genetically identical, for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions, four haploid cells, genetically different, for making gametes.
items.markingKey: Mitosis: one division, two diploid daughter cells, genetically identical, for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions, four haploid cells, genetically different, for making gametes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A force is needed to keep an object moving at constant speed." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A resultant force is needed only to change velocity; at constant speed forces are balanced (driving force equals resistance).
items.markingKey: A resultant force is needed only to change velocity; at constant speed forces are balanced (driving force equals resistance). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A class is planning an investigation into whether drawing coloured beads from two bags (to model gametes from two heterozygous parents) gives a ratio closer to 3 : 1 as the number of draws increases.
(a) Write a focused research question. [1]
(b) Explain how the independent variable will be changed, giving a suitable range. [1]
(c) Describe how the dependent variable will be measured and how many repeats are needed. [2]
(d) Explain how number of each colour in each bag (equal numbers) will be controlled and why. [1]
(e) Identify one safety or ethical consideration. [1]
items.answer: (a) How does number of pairs of beads drawn affect ratio of “dominant” to “recessive” phenotypes? (b) number of pairs of beads drawn (10, 20, 50, 100, 200) – at least five values across a sensible range. (c) ratio of “dominant” to “recessive” phenotypes – counted from the bead pairs and calculated as x : 1; at least three repeats and a mean. (d) number of each colour in each bag (equal numbers) – models a heterozygous parent producing 50% of each gamete. (e) pick up any spilled beads to avoid slipping.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 names IV and DV. (b) 1 method of changing the IV with ≥5 values. (c) 1 measurement method with instrument/units; 1 ≥3 repeats and mean. (d) 1 how and why number of each colour in each bag (equal numbers) is controlled (models a heterozygous parent producing 50% of each gamete). (e) 1 relevant point, e.g. pick up any spilled beads to avoid slipping.

items.stem:
A class is planning an investigation into how the number of hours of sleep the night before affects the reaction time of students measured with a ruler-drop test.
(a) Write a focused research question. [1]
(b) Explain how the independent variable will be changed, giving a suitable range. [1]
(c) Describe how the dependent variable will be measured and how many repeats are needed. [2]
(d) Explain how caffeine intake will be controlled and why. [1]
(e) Identify one safety or ethical consideration. [1]
items.answer: (a) How does hours of sleep the night before affect reaction time? (b) hours of sleep the night before (recorded by a sleep app) – at least five values across a sensible range. (c) reaction time – catch distance in cm on a 30 cm ruler, converted to time using t = √(2d/g); at least three repeats and a mean. (d) caffeine intake – caffeine affects synapses. (e) keep fingers clear of the ruler edge; use a plastic ruler.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 names IV and DV. (b) 1 method of changing the IV with ≥5 values. (c) 1 measurement method with instrument/units; 1 ≥3 repeats and mean. (d) 1 how and why caffeine intake is controlled (caffeine affects synapses). (e) 1 relevant point, e.g. keep fingers clear of the ruler edge; use a plastic ruler.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate whether the angle of reflection is always equal to the angle of incidence for a plane mirror. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Draw a line and a normal on paper; place the mirror on the line; shine a narrow ray from a ray box at 10°; mark the reflected ray with two crosses; measure r; repeat to 80°; repeat the whole set twice; plot r against i.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (ray boxes get hot; do not look directly into the beam). Model: Draw a line and a normal on paper; place the mirror on the line; shine a narrow ray from a ray box at 10°; mark the reflected ray with two crosses; measure r; repeat to 80°; repeat the whole set twice; plot r against i.

items.stem:
A class is planning an investigation into the percentage by mass of magnesium in magnesium oxide, to compare with the value calculated from the formula MgO.
(a) Write a focused research question. [1]
(b) Explain how the independent variable will be changed, giving a suitable range. [1]
(c) Describe how the dependent variable will be measured and how many repeats are needed. [2]
(d) Explain how heating to constant mass will be controlled and why. [1]
(e) Identify one safety or ethical consideration. [1]
items.answer: (a) How does mass of magnesium used affect percentage of magnesium in the oxide? (b) mass of magnesium used (several different masses, to test whether the percentage is constant) – at least five values across a sensible range. (c) percentage of magnesium in the oxide = mass of Mg ÷ mass of MgO × 100; at least three repeats and a mean. (d) heating to constant mass – all Mg must react. (e) do not look directly at burning magnesium; use tongs.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 names IV and DV. (b) 1 method of changing the IV with ≥5 values. (c) 1 measurement method with instrument/units; 1 ≥3 repeats and mean. (d) 1 how and why heating to constant mass is controlled (all Mg must react). (e) 1 relevant point, e.g. do not look directly at burning magnesium; use tongs.

items.stem:
Amara added 1.0 g of powdered metal to 25 cm³ of 0.5 mol/dm³ copper(II) sulfate solution and recorded the maximum temperature rise. Metals were placed in order of their position in the reactivity series (1 = magnesium, 2 = zinc, 3 = iron, 4 = lead).

Metal / position | Temperature rise / °C: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 32.4 | 31.8 | 32.7
2 | 13.2 | 13.7 | 8.8
3 | 7.8 | 8.3 | 8.1
4 | 2.3 | 2.2 | 2.2

(a) Identify the anomalous result and suggest one cause. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean temperature rise for each metal, ignoring the anomaly. [2]
(c) Describe the trend and explain it using scientific reasoning. [2]
(d) State whether the data support the hypothesis that "The temperature rise is largest for magnesium and decreases for zinc, iron and lead." and justify your answer. [1]
items.answer: (a) 8.8 at 2 position. (b) 1 position: 32.30, 2 position: 13.45, 3 position: 8.07, 4 position: 2.23. (c) The temperature rise is largest for magnesium and decreases for zinc, iron and lead. The further apart two metals are in the reactivity series, the more energy is released when one displaces the other, so the reaction is more exothermic. (d) Supported: the means follow the predicted pattern across the range.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 anomaly 8.8 with a plausible cause (misreading, timing error, uncontrolled variable). (b) M1 method, A1 all means correct: 1 position: 32.30, 2 position: 13.45, 3 position: 8.07, 4 position: 2.23 °C. (c) 1 trend with data, 1 scientific explanation: The further apart two metals are in the reactivity series, the more energy is released when one displaces the other, so the reaction is more exothermic. (d) 1 justified conclusion referring to the processed data.

items.stem:
Zara measured the magnetic field strength at different distances from the pole of a bar magnet using a phone magnetometer app.

Distance from pole / cm | Field strength / μT: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 465.9 | 452.3 | 453.2
4 | 57.3 | 59.1 | 56.8
6 | 16.9 | 17.2 | 16.4
8 | 7.2 | 9.7 | 7.4
10 | 3.7 | 3.7 | 3.6

(a) Identify the anomalous result and suggest one cause. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean field strength for each distance from pole, ignoring the anomaly. [2]
(c) Describe the trend and explain it using scientific reasoning. [2]
(d) State whether the data support the hypothesis that "The field strength falls rapidly as distance increases; doubling the distance reduces it to about one-eighth." and justify your answer. [1]
items.answer: (a) 9.7 at 8 cm. (b) 2 cm: 457.13, 4 cm: 57.73, 6 cm: 16.83, 8 cm: 7.30, 10 cm: 3.67. (c) The field strength falls rapidly as distance increases; doubling the distance reduces it to about one-eighth. Field lines spread out further from the pole, so the field is weaker; for a magnet the field falls roughly with the cube of distance. (d) Supported: the means follow the predicted pattern across the range.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 anomaly 9.7 with a plausible cause (misreading, timing error, uncontrolled variable). (b) M1 method, A1 all means correct: 2 cm: 457.13, 4 cm: 57.73, 6 cm: 16.83, 8 cm: 7.30, 10 cm: 3.67 μT. (c) 1 trend with data, 1 scientific explanation: Field lines spread out further from the pole, so the field is weaker; for a magnet the field falls roughly with the cube of distance. (d) 1 justified conclusion referring to the processed data.

items.stem:
Hana used a Geiger counter (with the background count subtracted) to measure the count rate from a beta source (beta particles are high-speed electrons emitted from the nucleus) through different thicknesses of aluminium.

Aluminium thickness / mm | Count rate / counts per minute: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.0 | 941 | 906 | 922
0.5 | 463 | 448 | 468
1.0 | 152 | 226 | 237
1.5 | 112 | 109 | 116
2.0 | 58 | 58 | 58

(a) Identify the anomalous result and suggest one cause. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean count rate for each aluminium thickness, ignoring the anomaly. [2]
(c) Describe the trend and explain it using scientific reasoning. [2]
(d) State whether the data support the hypothesis that "The count rate decreases as the thickness of aluminium increases, falling by roughly half for each 0.5 mm." and justify your answer. [1]
items.answer: (a) 152 at 1.0 mm. (b) 0.0 mm: 923.0, 0.5 mm: 459.7, 1.0 mm: 231.5, 1.5 mm: 112.3, 2.0 mm: 58.0. (c) The count rate decreases as the thickness of aluminium increases, falling by roughly half for each 0.5 mm. Beta particles are electrons that interact with the atoms of aluminium and are gradually absorbed; a few millimetres of aluminium stop almost all of them. (d) Supported: the means follow the predicted pattern across the range.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 anomaly 152 with a plausible cause (misreading, timing error, uncontrolled variable). (b) M1 method, A1 all means correct: 0.0 mm: 923.0, 0.5 mm: 459.7, 1.0 mm: 231.5, 1.5 mm: 112.3, 2.0 mm: 58.0 counts per minute. (c) 1 trend with data, 1 scientific explanation: Beta particles are electrons that interact with the atoms of aluminium and are gradually absorbed; a few millimetres of aluminium stop almost all of them. (d) 1 justified conclusion referring to the processed data.

items.stem:
Isabel collected boiling-point data (three sources) for the first five straight-chain alkanes, which are simple molecular substances.

Number of carbon atoms | Boiling point / K: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 99 | 100 | 101
2 | 175 | 168 | 224
3 | 203 | 210 | 212
4 | 239 | 251 | 249
5 | 276 | 270 | 273

(a) Identify the anomalous result and suggest one cause. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean boiling point for each number of carbon atoms, ignoring the anomaly. [2]
(c) Describe the trend and explain it using scientific reasoning. [2]
(d) State whether the data support the hypothesis that "Boiling point increases as the number of carbon atoms increases." and justify your answer. [1]
items.answer: (a) 224 at 2 . (b) 1 : 100.0, 2 : 171.5, 3 : 208.3, 4 : 246.3, 5 : 273.0. (c) Boiling point increases as the number of carbon atoms increases. Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces between them, so more energy is needed to separate them; the covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken. (d) Supported: the means follow the predicted pattern across the range.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 anomaly 224 with a plausible cause (misreading, timing error, uncontrolled variable). (b) M1 method, A1 all means correct: 1 : 100.0, 2 : 171.5, 3 : 208.3, 4 : 246.3, 5 : 273.0 K. (c) 1 trend with data, 1 scientific explanation: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces between them, so more energy is needed to separate them; the covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken. (d) 1 justified conclusion referring to the processed data.

items.stem: "The shell model of electron arrangement is a good enough model for MYP chemistry." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It is good enough for the first 20 elements and bonding at this level, as long as its limits are recognised.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains groups, periods, ion charges and bonding; simple to draw and use. Arguments against: does not explain elements beyond calcium (transition metals) well; electrons are not in fixed circular orbits; quantum model uses orbitals. Supported judgement: It is good enough for the first 20 elements and bonding at this level, as long as its limits are recognised. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: "Ultrasound should replace X-rays wherever possible in medical imaging." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Ultrasound should be used where it gives adequate images, especially in pregnancy, but X-rays remain necessary for bones and lungs.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: non-ionising, so safe for fetuses and repeated scans; real-time moving images; portable and cheaper. Arguments against: cannot image well through bone or air (lungs); image quality depends on operator skill. Supported judgement: Ultrasound should be used where it gives adequate images, especially in pregnancy, but X-rays remain necessary for bones and lungs. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A device in which an electromagnet repeatedly attracts a soft iron armature, breaking the circuit each time, so the hammer strikes a gong"?
items.answer: electric bell
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of electric bell.

items.stem: What is the momentum of a 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s?
items.answer: 20 000 kg m/s
items.markingKey: D. p = mv.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "reaction profile (energy level diagram)"?
options: A biological catalyst made of protein
A collision between reactant particles with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, leading to reaction
The theory that particles react only when they collide with enough energy (at least the activation energy) and the correct orientation
A graph showing the energy of reactants and products during a reaction, including the activation energy
items.answer: A graph showing the energy of reactants and products during a reaction, including the activation energy
items.markingKey: D. "reaction profile (energy level diagram)" is a graph showing the energy of reactants and products during a reaction, including the activation energy.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "virtual image"?
options: The distance from the centre of a lens to its principal focus
How loud a sound seems, determined by its amplitude
An image that cannot be projected onto a screen because the light rays only appear to come from it
How high or low a sound seems, determined by its frequency
items.answer: An image that cannot be projected onto a screen because the light rays only appear to come from it
items.markingKey: C. "virtual image" is an image that cannot be projected onto a screen because the light rays only appear to come from it.

items.stem: What is the weight of a 5 kg mass on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg)?
Which of the following best describes "double bond"?
options: Mass per unit volume of a substance, ρ = m ÷ V
A diagram showing the outer-shell electrons of the atoms or ions in a substance, with electrons from different atoms shown as dots and crosses
A lattice of millions of oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic forces in all directions, e.g. sodium chloride
A covalent bond in which two pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms, e.g. O=O
items.answer: A covalent bond in which two pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms, e.g. O=O
items.markingKey: D. "double bond" is a covalent bond in which two pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms, e.g. O=O.

items.stem: Explain why state symbols are useful in equations.
items.answer: They show the physical state of each substance, which tells you, for example, whether a gas is given off, a precipitate forms or a substance is in solution – information needed to carry out or understand the reaction.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They show the physical state of each substance, which tells you, for example, whether a gas is given off, a precipitate forms or a substance is in solution – information needed to carry out or understand the reaction. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why repulsion is the only true test for a magnet.
items.answer: A magnetic material and a magnet both attract a magnet, but only a magnet has poles that can repel another magnet’s like pole.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A magnetic material and a magnet both attract a magnet, but only a magnet has poles that can repel another magnet’s like pole. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why metals are good conductors of heat.
items.answer: Delocalised electrons gain kinetic energy and move through the metal, transferring energy quickly; vibrating ions also pass energy on.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Delocalised electrons gain kinetic energy and move through the metal, transferring energy quickly; vibrating ions also pass energy on. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between momentum and inertia.
items.answer: Inertia is the tendency to resist change in motion, depending on mass; momentum is mass × velocity, a vector that depends on how fast the object moves.
items.markingKey: Inertia is the tendency to resist change in motion, depending on mass; momentum is mass × velocity, a vector that depends on how fast the object moves. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
A class is planning an investigation into how the distance from a Wi-Fi router affects the signal strength received by a phone.
(a) Write a focused research question. [1]
(b) Explain how the independent variable will be changed, giving a suitable range. [1]
(c) Describe how the dependent variable will be measured and how many repeats are needed. [2]
(d) Explain how router channel and frequency band (2.4 GHz) will be controlled and why. [1]
(e) Identify one safety or ethical consideration. [1]
items.answer: (a) How does distance from the router affect signal strength in dBm? (b) distance from the router (1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 m) – at least five values across a sensible range. (c) signal strength in dBm read from a Wi-Fi analyser app; at least three repeats and a mean. (d) router channel and frequency band (2.4 GHz) – different bands behave differently. (e) Wi-Fi is non-ionising and low power; take care walking backwards in corridors.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 names IV and DV. (b) 1 method of changing the IV with ≥5 values. (c) 1 measurement method with instrument/units; 1 ≥3 repeats and mean. (d) 1 how and why router channel and frequency band (2.4 GHz) is controlled (different bands behave differently). (e) 1 relevant point, e.g. Wi-Fi is non-ionising and low power; take care walking backwards in corridors.

items.stem:
Nia is investigating the percentage by mass of magnesium in magnesium oxide, to compare with the value calculated from the formula MgO.
(a) State the independent variable. [1]
(b) State the dependent variable and how it will be measured. [1]
(c) Identify two control variables and explain why each must be kept constant. [2]
(d) Formulate a testable hypothesis and explain it using scientific reasoning. [2]
items.answer: (a) mass of magnesium used (several different masses, to test whether the percentage is constant). (b) percentage of magnesium in the oxide = mass of Mg ÷ mass of MgO × 100. (c) heating to constant mass – all Mg must react; minimal loss of smoke – loss of MgO lowers the oxide mass. (d) If the magnesium is fully converted to MgO, then the percentage by mass of magnesium will be 60%, because Mᵣ of MgO = 40 and Aᵣ of Mg = 24 (24/40 × 100).
items.markingKey: (a) 1: mass of magnesium used (several different masses, to test whether the percentage is constant). (b) 1: percentage of magnesium in the oxide = mass of Mg ÷ mass of MgO × 100 (must include how/units). (c) 1 each, variable + reason: any two of heating to constant mass (all Mg must react); minimal loss of smoke (loss of MgO lowers the oxide mass); the same balance (0.01 g) (precision); purity of ribbon (sanded) (oxide layer changes mass). (d) 1 for a testable if/then prediction linking IV and DV, 1 for correct scientific reasoning: If the magnesium is fully converted to MgO, then the percentage by mass of magnesium will be 60%, because Mᵣ of MgO = 40 and Aᵣ of Mg = 24 (24/40 × 100).

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the temperature of air affects the speed of sound. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): avoid very loud sounds near ears. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. avoid very loud sounds near ears); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem:
Nia is investigating how the depth of water in a ripple tank affects the speed of water waves.
(a) State the independent variable. [1]
(b) State the dependent variable and how it will be measured. [1]
(c) Identify two control variables and explain why each must be kept constant. [2]
(d) Formulate a testable hypothesis and explain it using scientific reasoning. [2]
items.answer: (a) depth of water (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 cm, measured with a ruler at several points). (b) wave speed = frequency (from the signal generator) × wavelength (from 10 wavelengths on the screen). (c) tank level (even depth) – uneven depth changes speed across the tank; frequency of the vibrator – speed calculated using v = fλ needs a known f. (d) If the water depth increases, then the wave speed will increase, because waves travel faster in deeper water (in shallow water v ≈ √(g × depth)).
items.markingKey: (a) 1: depth of water (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 cm, measured with a ruler at several points). (b) 1: wave speed = frequency (from the signal generator) × wavelength (from 10 wavelengths on the screen) (must include how/units). (c) 1 each, variable + reason: any two of frequency of the vibrator (speed calculated using v = fλ needs a known f); tank level (even depth) (uneven depth changes speed across the tank); lamp height (changes the magnification of the shadow pattern); water temperature (can change wave speed slightly). (d) 1 for a testable if/then prediction linking IV and DV, 1 for correct scientific reasoning: If the water depth increases, then the wave speed will increase, because waves travel faster in deeper water (in shallow water v ≈ √(g × depth)).

items.stem:
Jonas took cuttings from one parent pea plant, so all the plants were clones produced by mitosis. The clones were grown with different fertiliser concentrations and measured their height after 6 weeks.

Fertiliser concentration / g/dm³ | Plant height / cm: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 16.2 | 15.7 | 16.2
1 | 18.7 | 18.6 | 18.8
2 | 30.1 | 22.8 | 22.0
3 | 27.4 | 27.1 | 26.6
4 | 30.3 | 29.8 | 30.8

(a) Identify the anomalous result and suggest one cause. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean plant height for each fertiliser concentration, ignoring the anomaly. [2]
(c) Describe the trend and explain it using scientific reasoning. [2]
(d) State whether the data support the hypothesis that "Mean plant height increases as fertiliser concentration increases." and justify your answer. [1]
items.answer: (a) 30.1 at 2 g/dm³. (b) 0 g/dm³: 16.03, 1 g/dm³: 18.70, 2 g/dm³: 22.40, 3 g/dm³: 27.03, 4 g/dm³: 30.30. (c) Mean plant height increases as fertiliser concentration increases. The clones are genetically identical, so the differences are environmental: fertiliser supplies mineral ions such as nitrate for making proteins, so cells divide and grow more. (d) Supported: the means follow the predicted pattern across the range.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 anomaly 30.1 with a plausible cause (misreading, timing error, uncontrolled variable). (b) M1 method, A1 all means correct: 0 g/dm³: 16.03, 1 g/dm³: 18.70, 2 g/dm³: 22.40, 3 g/dm³: 27.03, 4 g/dm³: 30.30 cm. (c) 1 trend with data, 1 scientific explanation: The clones are genetically identical, so the differences are environmental: fertiliser supplies mineral ions such as nitrate for making proteins, so cells divide and grow more. (d) 1 justified conclusion referring to the processed data.

items.stem:
Tomás stretched a slinky spring along a smooth floor to different lengths and measured the speed of a longitudinal pulse by video analysis.

Stretched length / m | Pulse speed / m/s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 2.54 | 2.60 | 2.66

items.stem: "Electric cars are safer than petrol cars because they accelerate faster." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Faster acceleration is not in itself a safety advantage; safety depends on many design and behavioural factors.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rapid acceleration helps when merging or overtaking; low centre of gravity from batteries reduces rollover. Arguments against: high acceleration can lead to loss of control by inexperienced drivers; heavier cars cause more damage in collisions; safety depends mostly on driver behaviour, braking and design. Supported judgement: Faster acceleration is not in itself a safety advantage; safety depends on many design and behavioural factors. items.stem: "Average speed cameras are fairer than fixed speed cameras." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Average speed cameras measure what matters (speed over distance) and are fairer, though privacy and cost must be managed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: measure behaviour over a long stretch, not just at one point; drivers cannot simply brake at the camera; smoother traffic flow. Arguments against: expensive to install; privacy concerns from number-plate tracking; drivers may watch speedometer instead of road. Supported judgement: Average speed cameras measure what matters (speed over distance) and are fairer, though privacy and cost must be managed. items.stem: Explain why a change in a single base of a gene can lead to a genetic disorder.
items.answer: A changed base can change the triplet and therefore the amino acid; the protein may fold differently and stop working, e.g. sickle-cell anaemia from one base change in the haemoglobin gene.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a curve that levels off higher and a steep curve that levels off at the same height.
items.answer: A steeper curve with the same final value means a faster rate with the same amount of limiting reactant; a higher final value means more limiting reactant was used.
items.markingKey: A steeper curve with the same final value means a faster rate with the same amount of limiting reactant; a higher final value means more limiting reactant was used. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how blood glucose concentration is brought back to normal after a meal.
items.answer: The pancreas detects the rise and secretes insulin; insulin causes body cells to take up glucose and the liver to convert glucose to glycogen, so blood glucose falls back to normal (negative feedback).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The pancreas detects the rise and secretes insulin; insulin causes body cells to take up glucose and the liver to convert glucose to glycogen, so blood glucose falls back to normal (negative feedback). (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why an object can have a velocity of zero but still be accelerating.
items.answer: Acceleration depends on how velocity is changing; at the top of a throw a ball is momentarily at rest but its velocity is changing at 9.8 m/s² downwards.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Acceleration depends on how velocity is changing; at the top of a throw a ball is momentarily at rest but its velocity is changing at 9.8 m/s² downwards. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

(b) State the dependent variable and how it will be measured. [1]
(c) Identify two control variables and explain why each must be kept constant. [2]
(d) Formulate a testable hypothesis and explain it using scientific reasoning. [2]
items.answer: (a) drop height (0.50, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00, 2.50 m, measured with a metre rule). (b) fall time measured with light gates or an electromagnet release and trapdoor timer. (c) measuring height to the bottom of the ball – consistent distance; timer started exactly at release – systematic timing error. (d) If the drop height increases, then the fall time will increase in proportion to √height, because s = ½gt² for uniform acceleration from rest; a graph of s against t² will be a straight line with gradient g/2.

Mohammed predicts the outcome of an investigation into how the number of “undecayed” dice changes with each throw, to model the half-life of a radioisotope.

(b) Identify the independent and dependent variables. [2]
(c) State two variables that must be controlled. [1]
(d) Sketch the shape of the graph you would expect if the hypothesis is correct and explain how it would support the hypothesis. [1]
items.answer: (a) If the number of throws increases, then the number of dice remaining will decrease exponentially, with a constant “half-life” of about 3.8 throws, because each die has a fixed probability (1/6) of “decaying” per throw, like unstable nuclei. (b) IV: number of throws (time, 0 to 10 throws); DV: number of dice remaining after removing those showing a six (“decayed nuclei”). (c) throwing method; starting number of dice (100). (d) A graph of the DV against the IV showing the predicted trend; if the data follow this trend within the spread of repeats, the hypothesis is supported.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 testable prediction; 1 scientific reasoning: If the number of throws increases, then the number of dice remaining will decrease exponentially, with a constant “half-life” of about 3.8 throws, because each die has a fixed probability (1/6) of “decaying” per throw, like unstable nuclei. (b) 1 IV: number of throws (time, 0 to 10 throws); 1 DV: number of dice remaining after removing those showing a six (“decayed nuclei”). (d) A graph of the DV against the IV showing the predicted trend; if the data follow this trend within the spread of repeats, the hypothesis is supported.

items.stem: "Earthquake early-warning systems using P-waves are worth the cost." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For earthquake-prone cities the benefits in lives saved outweigh the costs, though they complement rather than replace strong building codes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: P-waves arrive before damaging S-waves, giving seconds of warning (e.g. Japan, Mexico); trains can be stopped and gas supplies shut off automatically. Arguments against: warning time is very short near the epicentre; false alarms reduce trust; expensive networks of seismometers. Supported judgement: For earthquake-prone cities the benefits in lives saved outweigh the costs, though they complement rather than replace strong building codes. items.stem: "Replacing petrol engines with electric motors in all vehicles would solve urban pollution." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Electric motors greatly reduce urban air pollution but do not eliminate it; the overall benefit depends on clean electricity and battery recycling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no exhaust emissions in cities, quieter streets; motors are about 90% efficient. Arguments against: brake and tyre particles still pollute; electricity may be generated from fossil fuels elsewhere; battery production has environmental costs.
